Setting custom colors

R uses a default color palate for colors
It is not ideal
You can override default colors with

scale_color_manual(): You define the colors
scale_color_brewer(): Use color scales from RColorBrewer
scale_color_viridis_<b|c|d>(): Use color scales from viridis

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups

Code

  scale_color_brewer()

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Brewer palates
The RColorBrewer is optimized for maps and has a variety of palates set using palette="<palate>"

Sequential (e.g., YlOrRd, PuRd)
Qualitative (e.g., Set3, Dark2)
Diverging (e.g., Spectral, PuOr)

A gallery is available in the R Graph Gallery

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Palettes
Viridis palates are designed

To be clear even if the viewer has common forms of colorblindness
To be clear when converted to greyscale
To have strongly contrasting colors with a logical order of progression

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Scales
The correct Viridis scale to use depends on your data:

scale_color_viridis_b()

Binned: Discrete with a defined order/ranking
Adjacent values have similar colors

scale_color_viridis_c()

Continuous: A range where any value is possible

scale_color_viridis_d()

Discrete: Discrete but unordered
Maximizes contrast between colors


What type of data do we have here?

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Colors
Viridis has several color range options

Set using option="<name>"
Possible names include magma, inferno, viridis, rocket, etc.

See all the options in the Viridis Documentation

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Other Important Viridis Options
The Viridis scale functions also have some other important options:

direction=[-1|1]

Sets the order of the colors. -1 reverses them

na.value="<color>"

Sets the color used when a value is NA
Set to NA for transparent

Setting Custom Colors - Manual
You may occasionally want to set manual colors

Use scale_color_manual()
Set the value= argument to a named vector
Each element of the vector is a "<value>"="<color>" pair

Best practices for setting colors

R’s default color choices are not ideal, particularly if more than a few colors
Both RColorBrewer and Viridis were designed by professionals
Use their palettes when possible

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Adjusting Legend Attributes
Many attributes of the way a legend is displayed are controlled by the plot theme

Change individual settings of the theme with theme()
Theme takes a series of named argument-value pairs
Named arguments define attributes of the theme
More complicated options controlled by guides()

See Tidyverse ggplot2 3.5.0: Legends for many examples

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Changing the legend position
The legend placement is controlled by theme attribute legend.position=

Possible values "left", "right", "bottom", "top"
"none" turns off the legend
"inside" requires legend.position.inside=c(x,y)

Places the legend inside at the specified x and y coordinates


Move the legend to the bottom of your visualization.

How does it change?

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
section: Move the legend to the bottom
text:
Move the legend to the bottom


Code
viz_wheat_color +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Group-level calculations

Recall that you can place mathematical expressions in aesthetics
R will evauluate them and use the result to define the data displayed
You can use summary functions like mean()
By default R will compute the summary over the full dataset
Add the group= aesthetic to perform the calculation over each group

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Group-level Calculations
There may be occasions where you would like to perform a calculation specific to each group and visualize that result

A few options

Use mutate() combined with if_else() or case_when()
Use group_by() and summary functions
Use group= along with calculations in an aesthetic


Let’s think about implementing the group= method

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Example of a Group-Level Calculation
What will the following code do?

ggplot(data=fao_wheat) +
  geom_line(mapping=aes(
    x=Year,
    y=(Value - mean(Value))/sd(Value),
    group=Area,
    color=Area
  ))

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Group-level Calculation in a Visualization


Code
ggplot(data=fao_wheat) +
  geom_line(mapping=aes(
    x=Year,
    y=(Value - mean(Value))/sd(Value),
    group=Area,
    color=Area
  )) +
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(
    title="Nordic Wheat Production",
    x="Year",
    y="Relative Production (z-score)",
    caption="Source: United Nations FAOSTAT",
    color="Country"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values=c(
      "Finland" = "#002F6C", #Finland blue
      "Sweden" = "#FECB00", #Sweden Yellow
      "Norway" = "#BA0C2F" #Norway Red
    )
  )

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Agricultural Productivity
How should we measure agricultural productivity?


Productivity is a measure of how inputs are converted into outputs

What are inputs to agriculture?



Land
Labor
Water
Machinery (capital)
Fertilizer
etc

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Measuring Agricultural Productivity
How do we measure agricultural productivity?

One measure is Total Factor Productivity
Index measuring how efficiently agricultural inputs are transformed into agricultural outputs
Effectively a ratio of output to inputs
Easy when there is one input
More difficult when there are many

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
TFP in Practice
In practice we measure TFP as a function

Hold other inputs/factors constant
TFP is the “left over” productivity

What is the difficulty with this approach?


How do we make sure farmers hold inputs constant? (we can’t)
Other factors (e.g., weather) are impossible to hold constant
Do we care about productivity in the lab or on real farms?

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Estimating TFP
Estimating TFP is an empirical modeling problem

Collect data on all factors we think influence crop growth
Across many farms and many years
Use of inputs and other factors will vary across observations
Use this variation to isolate the impact of each factor on output
Combine this with actual input use to predict output for each observation
TFP is the “residual” (true value minus prediction)

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Challenges with Measuring TFP

Suppose we want to compute the change in TFP for many countries over time
We’ll use the method I outlined

Collect data on output, inputs, and other factors
Use it to construct an empirical model of productivity
TFP is the residual unexplained by the model

What challenges might we encounter?
What might you do to address those problems?

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Some Challenges Measuring TFP
Some challenges measuring TFP using observational data

Consistency in measurement both across time and space
Unmeasured factors (e.g., intensity of rain)
Unmeasured quality of inputs and output
Substitution between inputs
Crop switching
Many more!

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Is Measuring TFP Impossible?

There are many ways our estimates of TFP could go wrong
No set of estimates is “perfect”
Should we just give up?



TFP estimates provide valuable information, even if not “perfect”
Do the best job we can
Continue to improve (better data, models, etc)

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Measuring National Agricultural Production
Consistency of data is important for measuring TFP across countries and over time

Ideally measure output using methods that allow for comparing measurements

Across all countries
Across time

Include the majority of countries
Include a wide array of agricultural products

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization

United Nations FAOSTAT Data
The UN collects and reports the FAOSTAT Data

Annual measurements of agricultural production
Consistent methods across over 200 countries/territories
Output measurements for nearly 300 types of output
Long time series of measurements (starting in 1961)

Available at https://www.fao.org/faostat
On Google Drive in Data/FAO

TFP in Practice
In practice we measure TFP as a function

Hold other inputs/factors constant
TFP is the “left over” productivity

What is the difficulty with this approach?


How do we make sure farmers hold inputs constant? (we can’t)
Other factors (e.g., weather) are impossible to hold constant
Do we care about productivity in the lab or on real farms?

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization

Estimating TFP
Estimating TFP is an empirical modeling problem

Collect data on all factors we think influence crop growth
Across many farms and many years
Use of inputs and other factors will vary across observations
Use this variation to isolate the impact of each factor on output
Combine this with actual input use to predict output for each observation
TFP is the “residual” (true value minus prediction)

section: CSV has been a de facto standard for data
text:
CSV has been a de facto standard for data
The Bottleneck:

Modern datasets like high-resolution climate rasters or satellite indices overwhelm plain text formats like CSV

e.g., The FAO data is nearly 400 MB in CSV format

Data stored in purely text format

Requires software “guess” properties of the data
Numeric data needs to be translated from text
Repeated text values written out in full, each time

CSV files are

Slow to read
Large
Require guesses or manual intervention to read correctly

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Modern Big Data Storage
The Next Generation:
Define a data file format for modern big data

Portable: Works across data processing systems
Fast: Information you need loads quickly
Compact: Data stored efficiently for small files
Consistent: All software interprets the data identically without guessing

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
The Parquet Format
Parquet (PAR-kay) is a modern data file format for storing tidy data frames

Created in 2013
Specification is free and open source
Managed by the Apache Foundation
Implemented in most data analysis software

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Column-orientation
Column-oriented storage

In CSV files data are oriented in rows

You must read all of one row before moving on to the next
Inefficient if you only want data from specific columns

Parquet files use a column format

Only need to read data for the columns you request

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Automatic Compression
Automatic Compression

A CSV must write out every value in every cell as text
Parquet automatically compresses information

Column-oriented files are more compressible in general
Dictionary compression of frequent values
Run-length encoding for repeated values
Delta-encoding efficiently packs sequential numbers/timestamps

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Strict Schema
Strict Schema

A CSV file doesn’t contain any information about data types
Parquet files explicitly define data types of each column

Integer, Floating point, Character, Boolean, Date, and Timestamp data types

Parquet uses explicit formats for each data type (e.g., IEEE-754 floating point)
Any data processing package interprets each value the exact same way
Explicit support for missing (NA) values

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Disadvantages

Binary files aren’t human-readable
Column-oriented format makes “appending” data slow

Poorly suited for cases where you frequently update data

Performance gains only materialize on larger files

1000s of observations
10s or 100s of columns

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:

Parquet much smaller, so they load quickly

Choosing a Visualization File Format
You have several choices for file formats, which have advantages and disadvantages

PDF files best for publication quality graphics

Are vector images, they scale up flawlessly to very large image sizes
Complicated visualizations make large output file that load slowly

PNG files best for general use

Are raster images, they will get blocky as you scale them up
Files will be a fixed size no matter how complicated the visualization

JPG files best for websites/text messages

Also raster images but use Lossy Compression
Files tend to be very small, nearly anyone can view them
Underlying compression algorithm can lose details

There are other, more niche formats available too

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Setting custom colors

R uses a default color palate for colors
It is not ideal
You can override default colors with

scale_color_manual(): You define the colors
scale_color_brewer(): Use color scales from RColorBrewer
scale_color_viridis_<b|c|d>(): Use color scales from viridis

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Setting custom colors - Brewer
By default Brewer uses blue colors and intensity


Code
viz_wheat_color + 
  scale_color_brewer()

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Brewer palates
The RColorBrewer is optimized for maps and has a variety of palates set using palette="<palate>"

Sequential (e.g., YlOrRd, PuRd)
Qualitative (e.g., Set3, Dark2)
Diverging (e.g., Spectral, PuOr)

A gallery is available in the R Graph Gallery

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Setting custom colors - Brewer Set3
Set3 is a categorical scale


Code
viz_wheat_color + 
  scale_color_brewer(palette="Set3")

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Setting custom colors - Viridis
Here is Viridis D


Code
viz_wheat_color + 
  scale_color_viridis_d()

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Palettes
Viridis palates are designed

To be clear even if the viewer has common forms of colorblindness
To be clear when converted to greyscale
To have strongly contrasting colors with a logical order of progression

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Scales
The correct Viridis scale to use depends on your data:

scale_color_viridis_b()

Binned: Discrete with a defined order/ranking
Adjacent values have similar colors

scale_color_viridis_c()

Continuous: A range where any value is possible

scale_color_viridis_d()

Discrete: Discrete but unordered
Maximizes contrast between colors


What type of data do we have here?

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Colors
Viridis has several color range options

Set using option="<name>"
Possible names include magma, inferno, viridis, rocket, etc.

See all the options in the Viridis Documentation

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Other Important Viridis Options
The Viridis scale functions also have some other important options:

direction=[-1|1]

Sets the order of the colors. -1 reverses them

na.value="<color>"

Sets the color used when a value is NA
Set to NA for transparent

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Setting Custom Colors - Manual
You may occasionally want to set manual colors

Use scale_color_manual()
Set the value= argument to a named vector
Each element of the vector is a "<value>"="<color>" pair
e.g., "Sweden"="yellow"

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Setting Customs Colors - Manual, easy
Set colors for each country to a color like one in their flag.


Code
viz_wheat_color + 
  scale_color_manual(
    values=c(

      # And the the name of color in their flag
      "Finland" = "blue", #Finland blue
      "Sweden" = "yellow", #Sweden Yellow
      "Norway" = "red" #Norway Red

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Best practices for setting colors

R’s default color choices are not ideal, particularly if more than a few colors
Both RColorBrewer and Viridis were designed by professionals
Use their palettes when possible
Only manually define colors if a specific color is important

Legend Defaults
By default, ggplot

Titles the legend after the corresponding aesthetic (e.g., “color”)
Places it on the right in vertical format

These defaults are not always optimal

Changing the legend title

You can change the legend title in labs()
The label name is the name of the corresponding aesthetic (e.g., “color”)
e.g., labs(color="Country")

text:
Adjusting Legend Attributes
Many attributes of the way a legend is displayed are controlled by the plot theme

Change individual settings of the theme with theme()
Theme takes a series of named argument-value pairs
Named arguments define attributes of the theme
More complicated options controlled by guides()

See Tidyverse ggplot2 3.5.0: Legends for many examples

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Changing the legend position
The legend placement is controlled by theme attribute legend.position=

Possible values "left", "right", "bottom", "top"
"none" turns off the legend
"inside" requires legend.position.inside=c(x,y)

Places the legend inside at the specified x and y coordinates


Move the legend to the bottom of your visualization.

How does it change?

text:
Group-level calculations

Recall that you can place mathematical expressions in aesthetics
R will evauluate them and use the result to define the data displayed
You can use summary functions like mean()
By default R will compute the summary over the full dataset
Add the group= aesthetic to perform the calculation over each group

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Group-level Calculations
There may be occasions where you would like to perform a calculation specific to each group and visualize that result

A few options

Use mutate() combined with if_else() or case_when()
Use group_by() and summary functions
Use group= along with calculations in an aesthetic


Let’s think about implementing the group= method

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Example of a Group-Level Calculation
What will the following code do?

ggplot(data=fao_wheat) +
  geom_line(mapping=aes(
    x=Year,
    y=(Value - mean(Value))/sd(Value),
    group=Area,
    color=Area
  ))

text:
Group-level Calculation in a Visualization


Code
ggplot(data=fao_wheat) +
  geom_line(mapping=aes(

section: Combining Data from Multiple Data Frames
text:
Combining Data from Multiple Data Frames
Think about two data frames that may contain similar information

Separate files for different measurements (e.g., CRU)
Separate files for different time periods
Separate files for different places

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Tidyverse methods for combining data
The tidyverse has several methods of combining data frames

bind_rows() stacks rows of data frames
bind_cols() stacks columns of data frames
Joins use more complicated logic to match rows between datasets

Covered next week

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Stacking Rows
bind_rows() stacks rows of multiple data frames

Each data frame is added to the bottom of the previous data frame
Useful when you have multiple data frames with the same layout

Identical column names
Identical data types

e.g.,

One data frame for each year of data
Otherwise identical

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Stacking Rows
bind_rows()

Returns a single data frame, aligning columns by name
Fills in with NA when a column doesn’t exist







Watch out for inconsistent data types!


Each column needs a single data type. R will attempt to coerce values of each column to a single data type, but won’t convert numbers to text or vice versa. This can lead to unexpected NA values if you try to stack a column that switches between text and numeric data!

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Two ways to use bind_rows()


Just stack data frames
bind_rows(data_2000,data_2001)




Stack rows from each data fame
But otherwise no way to tell them apart



Stack with identifier column
bind_rows(
  list(
    "2000" = data_2000, 
    "2001" = data_2001
  ),
  .id="Year"
)
Adds a Year column with the corresponding name from the list()

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Stacking Columns
bind_cols() stacks columns of multiple data frames

Each data frame is added to the right of the previous data frame
Useful when you have multiple data frames of information for the same observations

Observations align perfectly across each data frame
Column names do not overlap

e.g., a wide table was split up into multiple files

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Stacking Columns
In general you won’t use bind_rows()

Few cases where you need to combine columns across data frames by matching rows
Only useful when you have full knowledge of the provenance of each data frame, e.g.,

You intentionally split off columns from a data frame
Want to combine back later

No checks for whether observations are correctly aligned
Usually use Joins to match observations across dataframes (next week)

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Reshaping Data Overview
What does it mean to reshape (pivot) data?


Take information organized by columns and reorganize in rows or vice-versa
Will change the shape of your data frame

pivot_longer()

New data are longer and narrower
More rows, fewer columns
Column information translated into rows

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Reshaping Data Overview
What does it mean to reshape (pivot) data?
pivot_wider()

New data are wider and narrower
More columns, fewer rows
Row information is translated into columns

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Reshaping Data - The Old Way

The pivot functions are relatively new
The tidyverse previously used gather and spread
They have the superseded lifecycle tag
No new features will be added, but won’t be removed soon
Harder to use, Fewer features
Avoid using them

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Using pivot_wider()
When you use pivot_wider() you should ask yourself three questions:

Which column(s) will uniquely identify observation in my new data frame? id_cols
Which column(s) contain information that will be used to construct new column names? names_from
Which column(s) contain values that will populate those new columns? values_from

Each answer tells you what to use for each of the required arguments!

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Example pivot_wider()
I would like to create a new version of the CRU data frame

One row for each Country-Year
Columns for the temperature in each month

How can I do this?

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Example pivot_wider()

One row for each Country-Year
Columns for the temperature in each month


Which column(s) will uniquely identify observation in my new data frame? id_cols
Which column(s) contain information that will be used to construct new column names? names_from
Which column(s) contain values that will populate those new columns? values_from

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Example pivot_wider()

id_cols = c(Year,Country)
names_from = Period
values_from = Value







Remove extra columns before pivoting


When pivot_wider() rearranges your data frame it needs to know what to do with information in each column. This is ambiguous for any column that doesn’t show up in one of the three arguments. You should remove columns that aren’t needed with select() before pivoting.

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Implement pivot_wider()
Reshape the CRU data to make month columns

Remember to remove unneeded columns
id_cols = c(Year,Country)
names_from = Month
values_from = Value

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
section: CSV has been a de facto standard for data
text:
CSV has been a de facto standard for data
The Bottleneck:

Modern datasets like high-resolution climate rasters or satellite indices overwhelm plain text formats like CSV

e.g., The FAO data is nearly 400 MB in CSV format

Data stored in purely text format

Requires software “guess” properties of the data
Numeric data needs to be translated from text
Repeated text values written out in full, each time

CSV files are

Slow to read
Large
Require guesses or manual intervention to read correctly

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Modern Big Data Storage
The Next Generation:
Define a data file format for modern big data

Portable: Works across data processing systems
Fast: Information you need loads quickly
Compact: Data stored efficiently for small files
Consistent: All software interprets the data identically without guessing

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
The Parquet Format
Parquet (PAR-kay) is a modern data file format for storing tidy data frames

Created in 2013
Specification is free and open source
Managed by the Apache Foundation
Implemented in most data analysis software

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Column-orientation
Column-oriented storage

In CSV files data are oriented in rows

You must read all of one row before moving on to the next
Inefficient if you only want data from specific columns

Parquet files use a column format

Only need to read data for the columns you request

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Automatic Compression
Automatic Compression

A CSV must write out every value in every cell as text
Parquet automatically compresses information

Column-oriented files are more compressible in general
Dictionary compression of frequent values
Run-length encoding for repeated values
Delta-encoding efficiently packs sequential numbers/timestamps

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Strict Schema
Strict Schema

A CSV file doesn’t contain any information about data types
Parquet files explicitly define data types of each column

Integer, Floating point, Character, Boolean, Date, and Timestamp data types

Parquet uses explicit formats for each data type (e.g., IEEE-754 floating point)
Any data processing package interprets each value the exact same way
Explicit support for missing (NA) values

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Disadvantages

Binary files aren’t human-readable
Column-oriented format makes “appending” data slow

Poorly suited for cases where you frequently update data

Performance gains only materialize on larger files

1000s of observations
10s or 100s of columns

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet in this Class
In this class I will provide Parquet versions of most data files

Data files contain many, repeated text values
Very large CSV files
Parquet much smaller, so they load quickly
Strict schema, so everyone gets the same data
ELMS and gmail understand they are data files

Using ggsave
To save a visualization use
ggsave(<output_path>)

R determines the output format using the file extension

e.g., .png, .jpg, .pdf

Some important optional arguments are:

plot: A variable containing the plot to save

Otherwise, the default is the last plot generated

width: Width of the saved image in inches
height: Height of the saved image in inches

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Choosing a Visualization File Format
You have several choices for file formats, which have advantages and disadvantages

PDF files best for publication quality graphics

Are vector images, they scale up flawlessly to very large image sizes
Complicated visualizations make large output file that load slowly

PNG files best for general use

Are raster images, they will get blocky as you scale them up
Files will be a fixed size no matter how complicated the visualization

JPG files best for websites/text messages

Also raster images but use Lossy Compression
Files tend to be very small, nearly anyone can view them
Underlying compression algorithm can lose details

There are other, more niche formats available too
